purpose: How a managed Wi-Fi provider productizes design-plus-hardware-plus-monthly-management into a per-AP/per-site subscription, shapes and prices that offer for restaurants, motels, offices, retail and multi-dwelling properties, splits the guest-network and operations-network value stories, positions honestly against one-time installers, and qualifies which venues to propose to and which to decline.
assumptions: no observed dataset supplied; all scores are heuristic priors

the provider is a small local or regional operator selling designed business Wi-Fi plus a monthly management, monitoring and support subscription to physical venues; carrier-scale or enterprise-campus managed networking is out of frame
every price, uptime figure, commission and market size is treated as a mechanism or a quantity measured per deal; no specific number in this KB is asserted as a factual rate

licensing, consumer-protection, auto-renewal, referral-fee and guest-data-collection obligations vary by place; each such point names the obligation class and defers to current rules in the operating jurisdiction
content is educational operating knowledge for the business operator, never personalized financial, legal, tax or insurance advice for a specific venue
exclusions: RF site survey execution, AP placement, SSID/VLAN segmentation, hardware platform selection, captive portal construction, cabling, installation, validation testing and documentation handoff — the Wi-Fi design, deployment and handoff KB owns that territory

remote monitoring and alerting, firmware hygiene, SLA operations and uptime reporting, live support-tier escalation, renewal and retention execution, and expansion to additional sites or adjacent services such as cameras and VoIP — the monitoring, management and SLA operations KB owns that territory
interception or inspection-for-resale of guest traffic, sale of guest identity or behavior data, and any captive-portal data collection that is not disclosed to the guest and agreed by the venue
stating invented monthly fees, uptime percentages, commissions or market sizes as fact; pricing appears only as the per-AP/per-site derivation mechanism and qualitative bands
assuming spectrum congestion, wall construction, cabling paths, power availability or code constraints for any specific site — those are facts a survey establishes
personalized financial, legal, tax or insurance advice to any specific venue owner or property board

competency_questions.question: What exactly does the monthly managed Wi-Fi fee buy, and how is that different from what a one-time installer sells?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: WAAS_OFFER_DEFINITION separates the recurring accountabilities from the one-time components, and ONE_TIME_INSTALLER_POSITIONING frames the lifecycle difference without smearing competitors

competency_questions.question: Which venue classes should a young managed Wi-Fi provider pursue first, and what does each class buy Wi-Fi to protect?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: VENUE_SEGMENT_MAP names each venue class's buyer, its must-not-fail workload, its scale band and a reasoned beachhead ranking

competency_questions.question: How do the guest-network and operations-network value stories differ, and which one should carry the subscription justification?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: GUEST_VS_OPS_VALUE_SPLIT states both stories with venue-recognizable failure examples and explains why the operations story anchors the recurring fee

competency_questions.question: How is the monthly price for a specific venue derived from per-site and per-AP components without quoting invented figures?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: SUBSCRIPTION_PRICE_MECHANISM enumerates the cost-floor components, what moves each, and the per-site base plus per-AP increment derivation done per deal

competency_questions.question: Which hardware funding model fits a given deal — customer-purchased, amortized into the subscription, or provider-owned — and what does each imply for term length and exit?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: HARDWARE_FUNDING_MODEL states the three models with their recovery and churn implications and CONTRACT_TERM_STRUCTURE ties term, renewal notice and exit mechanics to the chosen model

competency_questions.question: What does the monthly management scope include and exclude, and where does the ISP's responsibility end and the provider's begin?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: SERVICE_SCOPE_CONTRACT lists written inclusions and exclusions and ISP_DEMARCATION_CLARITY explains the demarcation and how an ISP outage is handled and communicated

competency_questions.question: How is the service tier ladder structured so a venue's real outage risk maps to a tier instead of bespoke one-off promises?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: TIER_LADDER_DESIGN describes the entry, standard and premium tiers, what belongs in each, and the rule that no tier promises response the operations bench cannot staff

competency_questions.question: What may the sales conversation claim and collect, and what is forbidden — from uptime claims to captive-portal guest data?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: ETHICAL_SALES_BOUNDARY states the verifiable-claim, disclosure-first and no-fear-selling rules and GUEST_PRIVACY_STANCE states the no-interception, no-sale and disclosed-collection commitments

competency_questions.question: How does the shaped offer differ for a restaurant or shop, a motel or multi-dwelling property, and an office, and who is the buyer in each?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: each venue-shaping node names the buyer, the anchor workload, the coverage and density texture, and the tier and funding model that class tends to need

competency_questions.question: Which site facts must wait for a survey, and how does the offer stay honest before the survey happens?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: SITE_FACTS_QUALIFICATION lists the survey-only facts, the coarse observables a pre-sale walk may collect, and the survey contingency every estimate must carry

competency_questions.question: When should the provider decline or walk away from a deal, and what evidence justifies the no-go?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: DEAL_QUALIFICATION_GATE states the go/no-go checks — real pain, floor-clearing price, authority to sign, expectation fit, service radius — and treats walking away as a legitimate outcome

competency_questions.question: Where do qualified venue leads come from, and how are referral arrangements and proof assets kept honest?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: REFERRAL_CHANNEL_SOURCING names the partner classes and the disclosed-referral mechanism and PROOF_WITHOUT_FABRICATION defines proof assets that contain no invented claims

competency_questions.question: What must a signable proposal contain before it can hand off to design and installation?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: PROPOSAL_ASSEMBLY lists the required contents — pain summary, tier, transparent price derivation, survey contingency, funding and term mechanics, scope, demarcation and privacy commitment — and the signature-triggers-survey handoff

competency_questions.question: How is a venue's real Wi-Fi pain established from its own evidence before any value pitch is made?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: BUYER_PAIN_DISCOVERY lists the evidence sources — staff-named dead zones, rush-hour drops, review mentions, POS outage memory — and the rule that absent real pain the honest answer is no pitch

glossary.definition: The productized bundle a managed Wi-Fi provider sells: a designed network, installed hardware, and an ongoing monthly management, monitoring and support subscription, sold as one accountable service per venue rather than as equipment plus a warranty.
The ceiling- or wall-mounted radio unit that serves client devices; the AP count set by the design is the natural scaling unit of both coverage and the subscription's per-AP price component.
The visitor-facing wireless network a venue offers customers, guests or tenants; its value is experience and reputation — coverage at every table or room, an easy join, and a brand-safe welcome.

The separated network that carries the venue's own workloads — POS terminals, card readers, kitchen printers, door locks, cameras, back-office machines; its value is continuity, and its outage cost is what justifies paying monthly.
The join page a guest sees before getting online; any data it collects (an email, a room number) must be disclosed to the guest on the portal and agreed to by the venue in the service terms.

The two components of the subscription price mechanism: a base amount per managed site covering platform, administration and a support allotment, plus an increment per installed AP covering its license share, replacement reserve and marginal support labor.

A funding model in which the provider retains ownership of the installed gear and the subscription funds it; strongest continuity story for the venue, heaviest balance-sheet load and recovery risk for the provider.

The boundary where the ISP's responsibility for the internet circuit ends and the managed Wi-Fi provider's responsibility for the on-premise network begins; the offer must make this line explicit before signature.
An apartment building or similar multi-tenant residential property where Wi-Fi is sold as property-wide amenity infrastructure to the owner or manager rather than unit by unit to residents.
An on-site service visit; expected truck-roll frequency and travel radius are recurring costs the price derivation must carry, and a reason service radius is a qualification criterion.

source_registry.description: heuristic prior estimates for managed_wifi_offer_and_target_venues work units in absence of supplied datasets
source_registry.citation_or_locator: heuristic prior; no external dataset supplied

nodes.definition: Define the product as a single accountable service per venue: a survey-driven network design, installed access points and gateway, and a monthly subscription under which the provider watches the network, fixes it remotely, makes agreed configuration changes, and replaces failing hardware per the funding model. The unit of sale is the managed site, not a box. The definition must separate the recurring wrapper — what the monthly fee buys every month for as long as the contract runs — from the one-time components (design and installation labor), because that separation is what distinguishes the offer from an installer's receipt plus a fading warranty, and it is the sentence the owner repeats to their bookkeeper when the monthly charge appears.

included: the recurring accountabilities the monthly fee buys
the managed site as the unit of sale
excluded: how monitoring is technically performed (operations KB)
how the network is designed and installed (design KB)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a run of support tickets or cancellation reasons showing buyers thought the monthly fee covered something the written offer never named

pros.claim: A written offer definition makes the monthly fee defensible at renewal because the venue can point at what it received
pros.example: a motel owner reads the definition line 'we watch, fix remotely, and replace failed units' next to the quarter's three resolved incidents and renews without a price fight

cons.claim: A broad definition quietly turns the subscription into an unpaid general IT contract
cons.example: the phrase 'we keep your technology running' invites tickets about the restaurant's aging office PC and its label printer

failure_modes: selling hardware with a vague support promise instead of naming the monthly accountabilities
letting each salesperson improvise a different definition so no two contracts promise the same service
acceptance_tests: the offer definition names the recurring accountabilities, the one-time components, and the unit of sale in language a venue owner can repeat back accurately
revisit_triggers: support tickets or cancellation reasons show buyers believed the fee covered something the offer never named
a new adjacent service (cameras, VoIP) pressures the definition to stretch

nodes.definition: Map the five target venue classes — restaurant, motel and small lodging, office, retail shop, and multi-dwelling property — by who signs (owner-operator, general manager, office manager, property manager or board), what the network must never fail at (card payments during Friday rush, in-room streaming for a paying guest, a tenant's work-from-home day), the typical AP-count scale band, the sales-cycle texture from a two-visit owner close to a months-long property-board decision, and which classes the young provider should beachhead in given its truck-roll radius and references. The map is built by walking local venues and reading their public reviews, not from assumed national statistics.

included: venue-class taxonomy with buyer and must-not-fail workload
beachhead ranking for a specific provider

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: close-rate and churn evidence by venue class contradicting the assumed beachhead ranking

pros.claim: A ranked map concentrates scarce sales hours where the offer fits and references compound
pros.example: three won diners on the same commercial strip make the fourth diner a warm call, while a scattered motel-office-retail spread produces no neighborhood proof

cons.claim: A map drawn from assumption rather than local walking ranks segments the local market cannot support
cons.example: beachheading on motels in a town whose four motels all sit inside a franchise brand's mandated Wi-Fi program

failure_modes: treating all venues as one market and pitching a generic network to everyone
ranking segments by imagined revenue instead of by fit, radius and reachable buyers
acceptance_tests: each venue class in the map names its buyer, its must-not-fail workload, a scale band, and a reasoned beachhead position
revisit_triggers: close-rate or churn evidence by venue class contradicts the assumed ranking
the provider's service radius or install capacity changes

nodes.definition: Hold the two value stories apart and know when to tell each. The guest-network story is visible and emotional: coverage at every table, booth and room, a join flow that does not gate the meal or the check-in, and a welcome page that carries the venue's brand instead of a router vendor's logo — its failure shows up in public reviews. The operations-network story is invisible and financial: the POS terminals, card readers, kitchen printers, door locks and cameras stay up, and an outage during service costs real revenue and staff chaos. The guest story opens doors; the operations story justifies a recurring fee, because a venue will cancel a nicety but not the thing that keeps payments flowing.

included: both value narratives with venue-recognizable failure examples
which story anchors the subscription in each conversation
excluded: the SSID/VLAN separation that implements the split (design KB)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: win/loss debriefs showing which of the two stories actually moved the buyer in each venue class

pros.claim: Anchoring the fee on operations continuity survives price scrutiny that a guest-comfort pitch does not
pros.example: a cafe owner who would drop 'nicer guest Wi-Fi' in a slow month keeps the service that kept card payments alive through the last outage

cons.claim: Leading only with guest Wi-Fi invites comparison to a consumer router on a shelf
cons.example: an owner answers the guest-experience pitch with 'my nephew set up a mesh kit at home for a fraction of that'

failure_modes: pitching one blended story so the buyer hears only the cheap-to-replace guest half
promising guest-experience outcomes (better reviews) the provider cannot attribute or control
acceptance_tests: each story is written with a failure example the target venue class recognizes from its own operation
revisit_triggers: win/loss debriefs show which story actually moved buyers in a venue class

nodes.definition: The first-class rules of sale this business runs on. Every claim in a pitch must be verifiable: no invented uptime percentages, no fabricated horror stories about a named competitor's installs, no security theater. Pricing mechanics are disclosed before signature — what moves the monthly fee, what happens at term end, what an exit costs. The outage-cost conversation uses the venue's own reported incidents and review mentions, never manufactured dread; telling a motel owner that criminals will raid guests' bank accounts unless she signs is fear-selling and is forbidden. Small owner-operators for whom this is a large recurring spend get plain-language terms and time to decide — no pressure-close on a signature that funds years of payments.

included: care for small and unsophisticated buyers

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a complaint, dispute or regulator inquiry traceable to a sales claim, or a signed deal that later unwinds over an undisclosed term

pros.claim: Disclosure-first selling produces accounts that renew instead of accounts that feel trapped
pros.example: an owner who understood at signature exactly what moves her fee does not churn angrily when adding two APs raises it

cons.claim: Refusing fear tactics and pressure closes lengthens some sales cycles and loses some deals to louder competitors
cons.example: a rival who claims guaranteed five-nines uptime closes the impatient buyer the honest pitch could not

failure_modes: quoting an uptime number the provider has never measured
burying the auto-renewal or exit-fee mechanics until after signature
scaring a non-technical owner with invented breach scenarios to force a close
acceptance_tests: every claim in the current pitch materials traces to something measured, documented or directly observable
a signed buyer can restate what moves their fee and what an exit costs without opening the contract
revisit_triggers: a complaint, dispute or regulator inquiry traceable to a sales claim
a signed deal unwinds over a term the buyer says was never explained

nodes.definition: Productize the privacy position instead of leaving it implicit: the provider does not intercept guest traffic, does not inspect it for resale, and does not sell guest identity or behavior data — full stop, written into the service agreement. Any captive-portal collection the venue wants (an email for a mailing list, a room number for support) happens only with the venue's informed decision and with on-portal disclosure the guest can read before connecting. The stance is also a differentiator: a restaurant can tell its customers their connection is not being mined. Data-protection and consumer-disclosure obligations are an obligation class that varies by place — verify current rules in your jurisdiction before designing any portal data collection.

included: no-interception and no-sale commitments as contract language
excluded: portal implementation and disclosure copy placement (design KB)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a change in data-protection or consumer-disclosure rules in the operating jurisdiction, or a venue request pattern the current stance cannot answer

pros.claim: A written no-mining commitment converts a compliance topic into a selling point venues repeat to their own customers
pros.example: a coffeehouse prints 'our guest Wi-Fi does not track or sell your browsing' on the table tent and treats it as part of its brand

cons.claim: Declining data-monetization revenue narrows the margin levers available on thin deals
cons.example: an analytics vendor's per-venue revenue-share offer for portal marketing data must be refused even in a month when cash is tight

failure_modes: signing a venue that quietly expects undisclosed guest email harvesting
marketing the privacy stance while a portal vendor's default settings collect more than the disclosure states
acceptance_tests: the service agreement contains the no-interception and no-sale clauses and requires on-portal disclosure for any collection
every live portal's actual collection matches its disclosure exactly
revisit_triggers: data-protection or consumer-disclosure rules change in the operating jurisdiction
a venue or portal vendor requests collection the current stance does not answer

nodes.definition: Establish the venue's actual Wi-Fi pain from its own evidence before shaping any offer: which dead zones staff name unprompted, whether the connection drops during the Friday dinner rush, what the venue's public reviews say about its Wi-Fi, how many times the card reader went down last quarter and for how long, how old the current gear is and who installed it, and who physically power-cycles the router today. The inventory is collected by asking and reading, not asserting — pull the venue's own review mentions and the owner's incident memory into a written pain list. When the walk finds no real pain — a small stable shop with three devices and no guest expectations — the honest output is that there is nothing to fix, which routes the lead to a no-pitch outcome rather than a manufactured one.

excluded: technical diagnosis of why the pain occurs (design KB)
the go/no-go economics decision (qualification gate node)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: won and lost pitches showing the pain inventory did or did not match what the venue actually valued

pros.claim: A pain inventory in the venue's own words makes the later proposal read like a mirror instead of a brochure
pros.example: quoting the owner's line 'every Friday around eight the card reader dies' back in the proposal's first paragraph

cons.claim: Evidence gathering costs unpaid pre-sale hours that opportunistic competitors skip
cons.example: an hour reading a motel's reviews and interviewing the desk clerk while a rival emails a generic quote the same morning

failure_modes: pitching from a generic pain list the venue does not recognize
inflating a minor annoyance into a crisis to justify the subscription
acceptance_tests: every item in the pain inventory traces to a staff statement, a review mention, or a recalled incident with a rough date
revisit_triggers: pitches built on the inventory repeatedly miss what the venue actually valued

nodes.definition: Encode the rule that spectrum congestion, wall and ceiling construction, existing cabling paths, available power, and local code constraints are facts about one specific building that only a survey establishes — never assumptions the offer bakes in. The pre-sale walk collects only coarse observables and labels them as such: approximate floor area and floor count, obvious interference neighbors like the adjacent venue's visible AP grid, whether drop ceilings exist, where the ISP handoff sits. Every AP-count estimate and every derived price built before the survey carries an explicit survey contingency stating that the design visit fixes the final count. This node is the offer-side twin of the survey the design KB executes: it governs what may be promised before that survey exists.

included: permitted coarse observables and their labeling
the survey contingency in every pre-survey estimate
excluded: performing the RF survey or placement design (design KB)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: post-survey AP counts and cabling findings diverging repeatedly from pre-sale walk estimates

pros.claim: Survey-contingent estimates protect both margin and trust when the building disappoints
pros.example: a plaster-and-lath dining room that needs two more APs than the walk suggested triggers the disclosed contingency instead of an awkward renegotiation

cons.claim: Buyers who want a firm number today read contingent estimates as hedging
cons.example: a retail owner comparing against an installer's fixed flyer price asks why the managed quote 'has an asterisk'

failure_modes: promising whole-building coverage from the sidewalk before anyone has measured anything
quoting a fixed AP count that the survey then raises, forcing a price walk-back at the worst moment
acceptance_tests: every pre-survey estimate in circulation carries the survey contingency and labels its observables as coarse
revisit_triggers: post-survey AP counts repeatedly diverge from walk estimates in one direction
a venue class shows a recurring hidden constraint the walk should start capturing

nodes.definition: Price as a mechanism derived per deal, never a rate card of invented numbers. The monthly fee is assembled from a per-site base — the monitoring platform seat, administration, and a remote-support allotment every managed venue consumes regardless of size — plus a per-AP increment carrying that AP's management license share, its slice of the hardware replacement reserve, and the marginal monitoring and support labor it adds, with the whole stack multiplied by tier depth. The expert knows what moves each component: AP count comes from the design, truck-roll expectation from the venue's distance and fragility, the reserve from the funding model, after-hours coverage from the tier. The floor is verified per deal by summing the recurring cost stack — licenses, amortized hardware where bundled, expected labor hours at the provider's loaded rate, reserve contribution — and the quoted fee must clear that floor with intended margin. Any number spoken to a buyer is the output of this derivation for their venue.

included: the per-site plus per-AP component structure
excluded: asserting any specific monthly figure as a market fact
renewal price management on live accounts (operations KB)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: deal-level margin reviews showing the derived floor missed a real recurring cost such as truck-roll frequency or replacement reserve draw

pros.claim: A component derivation lets the provider defend the fee line by line instead of negotiating a mystery number
pros.example: showing a skeptical office manager that removing after-hours coverage moves the fee down one named component rather than 'a discount'

cons.claim: Component pricing takes longer to produce than copying a competitor's flyer and can price out the smallest venues
cons.example: a two-AP kiosk whose honest floor exceeds what any kiosk would pay reveals a segment the offer cannot serve

failure_modes: quoting from a generic figure heard at a trade meetup instead of deriving the deal's floor
omitting truck-roll or replacement-reserve costs so the account loses money quietly for its whole term
acceptance_tests: every quoted fee has a written derivation worksheet whose cost-floor components are enumerated for that venue
no pitch material asserts a specific monthly price as a market fact
revisit_triggers: deal-level margin review shows the floor missed a real recurring cost
the funding model or tier contents change, moving component definitions

nodes.definition: Draw the written boundary of what the monthly fee covers so the managed Wi-Fi contract cannot drift into an unpaid general IT contract. Included, stated positively: network monitoring, remote troubleshooting of the managed gear, configuration changes within the delivered design (a new staff password, a renamed guest SSID), scheduled maintenance the operations team executes, and hardware replacement per the funding model. Excluded, stated just as plainly: the ISP circuit and its outages, guests' and staff members' personal devices, the venue's PCs, tablets and printers as endpoints, new cabling for a remodel, and feature additions that change the design — each excluded item named because it is the request most likely to arrive in month two. The scope sheet is a sales document and a contract exhibit at once.

included: the written exclusion list with the likely month-two requests named
scope as both sales sheet and contract exhibit

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the ledger of out-of-scope requests arriving in the first months of live accounts

pros.claim: Naming the likely month-two requests as exclusions up front converts scope fights into calm quotes
pros.example: when the restaurant asks the provider to fix its office laptop, the owner has already read 'staff computers are not covered' and accepts a separate arrangement

cons.claim: A visibly fenced scope can feel stingy next to a rival's vague 'we handle everything' promise
cons.example: a buyer chooses the competitor whose unwritten everything-promise later collapses, but the deal is still lost today

failure_modes: leaving scope verbal so every technician inherits a different promise
writing inclusions so narrowly that routine password changes become billable surprises that poison trust
acceptance_tests: the scope sheet lists inclusions and exclusions including ISP outages, endpoint devices and new cabling, and is attached to every proposal
revisit_triggers: the ledger of out-of-scope requests from live accounts shows a request class the sheet does not address
a new tier or adjacent service moves items across the boundary

nodes.definition: Structure service depth as a ladder of named tiers so a venue's real outage risk maps to a tier instead of to bespoke one-off promises scribbled in a margin. An entry tier covers the monitored network with business-hours remote support and next-scheduled-visit hardware swap — fit for a low-stakes shop. A standard tier adds priority remote response and included replacement — fit for venues where the operations network carries payments. A premium tier adds after-hours coverage and a response-time commitment, offered only where the monitoring bench the operations KB describes can honestly staff it. The ladder's discipline is the point: when a buyer asks for a custom promise, the answer is a tier that contains it or a decline, because twenty bespoke contracts cannot be operated by a small team.

included: tier contents and the risk-to-tier mapping
excluded: SLA legal drafting beyond tier contents

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the tier distribution of signed deals showing one tier absorbing almost all buyers or a tier that never sells

pros.claim: A small tier ladder keeps twenty accounts operable by one bench because every account is one of three known shapes
pros.example: the on-call technician knows every premium account gets after-hours response without reading twenty different contracts first

cons.claim: Tiers that fit the median venue pinch the outliers on both ends
cons.example: a tiny florist overpays in the entry tier while a 24-hour diner's real need sits awkwardly between standard and premium

failure_modes: selling a premium response commitment no one is staffed to honor at 2 a.m.
letting every deal negotiate custom terms until the tier ladder exists only on the website
acceptance_tests: each tier's contents are written, priced through the component mechanism, and every commitment in the premium tier is one the current bench can staff
revisit_triggers: signed deals cluster in one tier or a tier never sells
the operations bench's staffable coverage window changes

nodes.definition: Choose, per deal or as house policy, who pays for and owns the installed gear, because the answer shapes margin, churn resistance and exit mechanics. Customer-purchased upfront: the venue owns the APs, the provider margins the install, the monthly fee covers pure service — lowest recurring lock, cleanest exit. Amortized into the subscription: the buyer's cash outlay is smoothed into the term, the provider fronts the gear and bears recovery risk if the account exits early — the term must at least recover the amortized balance. Provider-owned hardware-as-a-service: the strongest continuity story ('we own it, we replace it, you never buy a router again') and the heaviest balance-sheet load. The mechanism teaching is what each model does at exit — walk away clean, pay off the remaining amortization, or return/buy out provider gear — and the rule that the applicable model is disclosed at signature, never discovered at cancellation.

included: the three funding models and their margin, churn and balance-sheet implications
disclosure of the applicable model at signature

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: early-cancellation events testing whether hardware recovery actually works as the chosen model designed it to

pros.claim: Amortized and provider-owned models remove the upfront-cost objection that kills small-venue deals
pros.example: a motel that balked at a five-figure install invoice signs when the same gear rides inside the monthly fee across the term

cons.claim: Fronting hardware concentrates early-churn risk on the provider's thin balance sheet
cons.example: a restaurant that closes eight months into an amortized deal leaves the provider holding installed gear and an unrecovered balance

failure_modes: amortizing gear into a term too short to recover it
leaving gear ownership ambiguous so cancellation becomes a dispute over who owns the ceiling APs
acceptance_tests: every signed deal names its funding model and its exit outcome in the agreement
revisit_triggers: an early-cancellation event tests whether hardware recovery works as designed
hardware cost or financing conditions shift the viability of fronting gear

nodes.definition: Set term length, renewal and exit as honest mechanics that follow from the funding model rather than as traps. Amortized or provider-owned gear needs a term long enough to recover the fronted hardware; customer-owned gear can run month-to-month or on a short term. Auto-renewal, where used, comes with advance written notice rather than silent rollover. Early exit is priced plainly in the agreement: the remaining amortized balance, or equipment return or buyout under provider ownership — never a punitive fee unmoored from real cost. Consumer-protection and auto-renewal notice obligations are an obligation class that varies by place — verify current rules in your jurisdiction before finalizing renewal clauses. The underlying position: the subscription should be retained by service quality, and a venue that genuinely wants out should be able to leave without litigation, because trapped accounts poison local reputation in a referral-driven trade.

included: term length as a function of funding recovery
jurisdictional obligation-class flag on renewal clauses
excluded: renewal and retention execution on live accounts (operations KB)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a renewal dispute on a live account, or a jurisdictional change to auto-renewal notice obligations

pros.claim: Exit terms priced at real cost turn cancellation conversations into arithmetic instead of fights
pros.example: a closing cafe pays the stated remaining amortization, returns nothing, and its owner still recommends the provider to her next venture

cons.claim: Fair-exit terms give up the revenue certainty that heavy termination fees manufacture
cons.example: a lender or buyer valuing the account book discounts contracts a venue can leave at real cost

failure_modes: a silent auto-renewal that locks a venue for another term it never chose
an exit fee so detached from real cost it invites a dispute and a consumer complaint
acceptance_tests: every agreement states term, renewal notice, and the exit arithmetic for its funding model, and renewal clauses carry the jurisdiction-check flag in the drafting checklist
revisit_triggers: a renewal dispute on a live account
auto-renewal notice obligations change in the operating jurisdiction

nodes.definition: Make the demarcation explicit in the offer itself: the managed service begins where the ISP hands off — the provider designs, watches and answers for everything from the gateway inward, while the internet circuit remains the ISP's product and the ISP's failure. The offer explains, before signature, exactly how an ISP outage will look (the Wi-Fi is up, the internet behind it is down), that the provider's monitoring can tell the difference and will say so honestly, and that helping diagnose and escalate to the ISP is a defined courtesy or add-on rather than silent absorbed liability. Told well, the boundary is a selling point — no more circular finger-pointing between an installer who blames the ISP and an ISP who blames the router — because one party now owns everything inside the building and can prove where a fault sits.

included: what an ISP outage looks like to the venue
escalation help as a defined courtesy or add-on
excluded: monitoring mechanics that localize a fault (operations KB)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the first ISP outage on a live account and whether the venue blamed the provider despite the explanation

pros.claim: A pre-drawn demarcation preserves trust on the first ISP outage instead of spending it
pros.example: the venue calls in a panic, the provider says 'your Wi-Fi is healthy, the cable circuit is down, here is the outage reference to give them' — and the relationship strengthens

cons.claim: A venue that wants one throat to choke may hear the demarcation as pre-arranged blame-shifting
cons.example: a non-technical owner asks 'so when the internet dies you'll just say it's not you?' and needs the honest-diagnosis promise spelled out

failure_modes: leaving the boundary unstated so every ISP outage becomes the provider's unpaid emergency
hiding behind the demarcation to dodge a fault that was actually inside the managed network
acceptance_tests: the proposal explains the demarcation and the ISP-outage experience in plain language before signature
revisit_triggers: the first ISP outage on a live account and whether the venue blamed the provider

nodes.definition: Frame the competitive difference truthfully: a one-time installer leaves the venue owning an unmonitored network whose slow degradation is discovered by customers during service, with help available at hourly rates whenever someone answers; the managed offer sells the lifecycle — someone watches the network, patches it, replaces what fails, and answers when it breaks. The positioning rules are as important as the frame: compare service models, never smear a named local installer (this is a small-town trade and today's rival is tomorrow's referral source); use total-cost-over-the-lifecycle and cost-of-an-outage-hour framing built from the venue's own numbers; and concede honestly when a one-time install is the right buy — a tiny stable venue with simple needs, or a business with capable in-house IT, should be told so and sold an install or nothing.

excluded: the qualification decision itself (qualification gate node)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a local one-time installer beginning to bundle monitoring or a rival managed offer entering the same territory

pros.claim: Conceding the cases where one-time install genuinely fits makes every other claim more believable
pros.example: telling a three-desk bookkeeping office 'a good install and no subscription is right for you' earns the referral that brings a forty-room motel

cons.claim: The lifecycle argument is abstract until the buyer has lived a failure
cons.example: an owner whose consumer router has not yet died hears 'ongoing management' as an extended warranty she always declines at checkout

failure_modes: winning the comparison by trashing a named local installer and poisoning the referral well
overclaiming against one-time installs so hard that the provider's own install-only work looks like an admission
acceptance_tests: positioning materials compare service models without naming and disparaging local competitors, and list the concession cases
revisit_triggers: a local one-time installer begins bundling monitoring, collapsing the differentiation

nodes.definition: Shape the offer for restaurants, cafes and retail shops: the operations anchor is POS and card-payment continuity through peak service, because a payment outage during the dinner rush is measured in walked tables and comped meals; the guest story is coverage at every table and a join that does not gate the visit. The venue texture is small AP counts with sharp density spikes at rush, back-of-house needs the owner forgets to mention (kitchen printers, the cramped office), and a buyer who is usually the owner-operator deciding in one or two visits on gut trust plus one proof point. Thin and seasonal margins shape the recommendation toward the standard tier and smoothed hardware funding; the pitch's proof is the venue's own review mentions and last quarter's card-reader incidents, not industry statistics.

included: restaurant/retail anchor workloads, density texture, buyer and cycle
tier and funding tendencies for the class
excluded: the rush-hour capacity design itself (design KB)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: win/loss reasons and first-quarter ticket patterns from restaurant and retail deals

pros.claim: Anchoring on payment continuity gives the smallest venues a concrete reason to pay monthly
pros.example: a taqueria owner who shrugged at guest Wi-Fi signs after recounting the Saturday the card reader died with a line out the door

cons.claim: Restaurant economics cap what the class can pay and its failure rate is the trade's highest
cons.example: a well-run account vanishes when the restaurant itself closes in month nine, taking the amortized gear recovery with it

failure_modes: selling only the guest story and losing to a consumer mesh kit
ignoring back-of-house coverage so the kitchen printer keeps dropping after go-live and sours the account in week one
acceptance_tests: the restaurant/retail offer sheet names the payment-continuity anchor, the rush-density texture, and the tier and funding tendency for the class
revisit_triggers: first-quarter ticket patterns from live restaurant accounts contradict the assumed anchor

nodes.definition: Shape the offer for motels, small lodging and multi-dwelling properties, where coverage per room or unit is the product itself: the guest who cannot stream in room 214 writes the review that costs bookings, and the tenant who cannot work from home leaves at lease end. The texture is property-wide scale (tens of APs across wings and floors), nightly guest turnover demanding a dead-simple join flow, bandwidth fairness so one unit cannot starve the rest, and — for lodging — the front desk's own operations network (locks, cameras, property systems) as the quiet second story. The buyer is a property manager, owner or board with a longer, more formal cycle than a restaurant close; the per-room or per-unit count gives the per-AP price mechanism its most natural handle, and property-wide scale usually argues for a longer term with amortized or provider-owned gear. For MDUs, the framing is amenity infrastructure that protects occupancy and rent positioning, not a telecom product sold to residents.

included: property-scale texture and the property-manager buyer
excluded: per-unit resident billing as a resold service (offer definition boundary)
the multi-floor RF design itself (design KB)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: occupancy-season feedback and review mentions from lodging accounts about in-room coverage and join friction

pros.claim: One property signature yields dozens of APs of recurring revenue and a portfolio door
pros.example: a management company happy with one forty-unit building brings its other three properties without a cold call

cons.claim: Property decisions move slowly and one board seat can stall a deal for a season
cons.example: an HOA board tables the amenity Wi-Fi vote to its next quarterly meeting, twice

failure_modes: quoting a property from the lobby without the survey contingency, then finding concrete wings that eat signal
promising per-room performance while ignoring bandwidth fairness so the review the offer was meant to prevent still gets written
acceptance_tests: the lodging/MDU offer sheet names per-room coverage as the product, the fairness expectation, the buyer and cycle, and the term and funding tendency for property scale
revisit_triggers: occupancy-season feedback or review mentions from live lodging accounts about in-room coverage
a property-manager buyer requests resident billing, pressing the amenity boundary

nodes.definition: Shape the offer for offices and professional suites, where the operations network is the whole product: VoIP calls that do not crackle, video meetings that do not freeze, and file access that does not stall are the workday, and guest Wi-Fi is a lobby courtesy rather than a selling point. The buyer is an office manager, practice administrator or fractional IT consultant who evaluates in writing and asks about security posture — the offer answers at the value level (guest access separated from the business network, no credential sprawl on sticky notes) while the implementing segmentation belongs to the design KB. Multi-tenant buildings add the who-pays question: landlord-provided building Wi-Fi versus per-suite service changes the buyer, the contract party and the scale, and must be settled during qualification, not discovered at install.

included: the written-evaluation buyer and security-posture expectations at value level
excluded: the VLAN and access-control implementation (design KB)
general managed-IT services beyond the network

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: office deals lost to in-house IT or to a managed-IT bundle that includes the network

pros.claim: Office accounts are stable, daytime-only and reference well to other professional tenants
pros.example: a dental practice's administrator introduces the provider to the law office upstairs after a quiet first year

cons.claim: Offices with in-house or contracted IT often only want an install, not a subscription
cons.example: a firm's IT consultant welcomes the wiring work but insists on holding management himself, exactly the concession case the positioning node names

failure_modes: pitching guest-experience value to a buyer who only cares that Monday's video calls hold
signing a tenant for building infrastructure the landlord controls
acceptance_tests: the office offer sheet names the ops-network anchor, the security-posture answer at value level, and the landlord-versus-tenant decision point
revisit_triggers: office deals lost to in-house IT or to bundled managed-IT competitors

nodes.definition: Build the lead engine from adjacent trades whose own work exposes bad venue Wi-Fi: POS dealers and restaurant-tech vendors (their terminals die on flaky networks and they are tired of the blame), electricians and low-voltage contractors already inside ceilings, property managers holding portfolios of buildings, and hospitality suppliers who hear operator complaints daily. The mechanism of a referral arrangement is defined, not improvised: what the partner receives (reciprocal referrals, or a disclosed fee where lawful — referral-fee treatment is an obligation class, verify current rules in your jurisdiction and the partner's industry), and the non-negotiable rule that the venue is told a referral relationship exists. Direct sourcing complements the channel: walking the beachhead neighborhoods and reading venues' public reviews for Wi-Fi complaints yields a pre-qualified call list no directory sells.

included: partner classes and what each sees
the disclosed-referral mechanism and its jurisdiction flag
excluded: renewal-driven expansion within existing accounts (operations KB)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: referral-source tracking showing which partner class produces deals that survive qualification and which produces noise

pros.claim: A POS dealer's referral arrives pre-sold on the operations story because the dealer's terminal was the victim
pros.example: the dealer introduces the provider with 'your network is why your terminal drops — these people fix that', collapsing weeks of pitch into one sentence

cons.claim: Channel leads inherit the partner's agenda and quality, not the provider's qualification standard
cons.example: an electrician forwards every customer who mentions Wi-Fi, including apartment tenants and home offices the offer does not serve

failure_modes: paying undisclosed kickbacks that surface later and burn both reputations
depending on one partner class so its slow season becomes the provider's empty pipeline
acceptance_tests: every active referral arrangement is written, discloses the relationship to the venue, and carries the jurisdiction-check flag where a fee is involved
revisit_triggers: referral-source tracking shows a partner class producing leads that fail qualification

nodes.definition: Build the proof the pitch stands on without inventing any of it. The core assets: a pilot venue instrumented from day one so before/after evidence is measured, not remembered; case references told with the venue's permission and in its own words; a live view of the monitoring dashboard shown as 'this is how we watch your network' (the tooling belongs to the operations KB, its demonstration belongs here); and written references a skeptical office manager can call. The prohibitions are as concrete as the assets: no uptime percentage the provider has not measured over a stated period, no stock-photo case studies, no implying a review-score improvement the provider cannot attribute, and when a young provider is asked for track record it does not have, the honest answer — 'we are new, here is our pilot's measured data and here is the owner's phone number' — is the asset.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the first measured before/after dataset from a pilot venue replacing assumed proof points

pros.claim: A live dashboard demo makes the invisible service visible at the exact moment the buyer doubts it exists
pros.example: showing the prospect the pilot cafe's APs green on screen, then a replayed alert from the night an AP failed and was swapped before breakfast

cons.claim: Honest proof accumulates slowly while competitors invent theirs instantly
cons.example: the pilot needs a full season to produce a defensible before/after story a rival fabricates in an afternoon

failure_modes: citing an uptime figure with no measurement window behind it
using a reference venue without its permission and losing the account when the owner finds out
acceptance_tests: every claim in the proof kit traces to a measured dataset, a permissioned reference, or a live demonstration
revisit_triggers: the first measured before/after dataset from a pilot replaces assumed proof points

nodes.definition: Run the gate before proposal effort is spent, and treat walking away as a legitimate outcome. The checks: does the venue have real, evidenced pain the offer actually fixes; does the derived price clear the cost floor while remaining credible against the venue's economics; is the site inside the truck-roll radius the service model can sustain; are expectations compatible with the offer (a buyer demanding a guarantee against ISP outages, or instant on-site response the tiers do not sell, is a mis-sale in progress); is the person across the table authorized to sign (tenant versus landlord, manager versus owner, franchisee versus corporate mandate); and is there an existing contract — an ISP bundle, a franchise Wi-Fi program — that blocks the deal regardless of merit. A no-go is recorded with its reason, because the pattern of no-gos is the map's error signal.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: post-mortems of accepted deals that became problem accounts within their first term

pros.claim: A hard gate keeps the young provider's scarce install and support capacity for accounts that can succeed
pros.example: declining a remote roadhouse an hour outside the radius protects response times for the twelve in-town accounts that reference each other

cons.claim: A strict gate starves a hungry pipeline and can rationalize timidity
cons.example: an ambiguous motel deal declined for expectation mismatch was in truth winnable with one more clarifying conversation

failure_modes: signing a below-floor deal for momentum that loses money every month of its term
proposing to a tenant whose landlord controls the building's wiring and internet
acceptance_tests: every proposal in flight has a completed gate record showing pain evidence, floor clearance, radius, expectation fit, authority and contract-conflict checks
revisit_triggers: an accepted deal becomes a problem account within its first term
no-go patterns cluster in one segment, implicating the map

nodes.definition: Assemble the venue-specific proposal that a qualified deal deserves and nothing less: the pain summary in the venue's own words at the top; the two-network value story tuned to the venue class; the recommended tier with its contents listed, not alluded to; the price shown as its derivation — per-site base, per-AP increment, tier multiplier — so the buyer sees the machine, not a number; the survey contingency stating that the design visit fixes the final AP count; the funding model and term with the exit arithmetic; the scope sheet as an exhibit; the ISP demarcation in plain language; and the guest-privacy commitment. Signature does two things at once: it forms the agreement and it triggers the survey-and-design handoff to the deployment KB, making the proposal the last artifact this subdomain owns.

included: signature as the survey handoff trigger
excluded: the survey and design work that follows signature (design KB)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: proposal-to-signature conversion rates and the clauses buyers question or strike most often

pros.claim: Showing the derivation in the proposal pre-answers the negotiation and shortens it
pros.example: instead of 'can you do better on price', the motel owner asks 'what if we do business-hours support only' — a question the component structure can answer honestly

cons.claim: A complete proposal is heavier to produce than a one-line quote and can overwhelm the smallest buyers
cons.example: a food-truck commissary owner glazes over at a multi-page document when two APs and a paragraph would have closed

failure_modes: sending a bare price that wins on a number the buyer misunderstood
omitting the survey contingency and eating the difference when the building disagrees with the walk
acceptance_tests: every issued proposal contains the pain summary, tier contents, derivation, survey contingency, funding and term mechanics, scope exhibit, demarcation explanation and privacy commitment
signature demonstrably triggers the survey handoff with the proposal attached as its input
revisit_triggers: proposal-to-signature conversion drops or buyers repeatedly question or strike the same clause
the design KB's survey intake changes what the handoff must contain

edges.why_related: the segment map ranks venues by fit against the offer the definition fixes
the two value stories articulate what the defined offer is worth to whom
the scope sheet operationalizes the offer definition into contract inclusions and exclusions
which network story is promised shapes what the scope must include for each network
the price derivation prices exactly the scope's inclusions, nothing outside them
tier prices are produced by the component mechanism at different service depths
the funding model decides whether amortized hardware sits inside the derived monthly components
term length must recover fronted hardware, so the funding choice precedes term drafting
the demarcation is the scope sheet's most consequential exclusion, drawn out into its own pre-signature explanation
pain discovery asks the questions the segment map says matter for that venue class
the pain conversation happens first; the coarse site walk and its survey-contingent estimate follow it
the restaurant/retail shaping instantiates the map's entry for that class
the lodging/MDU shaping instantiates the map's entry for property-scale venues
the office shaping instantiates the map's entry for professional tenants
the restaurant recommendation points at a tier, so the ladder must exist first
property-scale deals select tiers and terms off the ladder rather than negotiating bespoke service
office recommendations map the class's reliability needs onto existing tiers
partner classes are chosen for their reach into the beachhead segments the map ranks
the gate's first check consumes the evidenced pain inventory
the gate needs the coarse site observables and contingency status to judge feasibility honestly
the gate's floor-clearance check runs the deal through the price derivation
only a deal that passes the gate earns the effort of a full proposal
the proposal presents the term, renewal and exit arithmetic the structure defines
the privacy commitment is a required proposal section, not an optional appendix
the plain-language demarcation explanation must appear in the proposal before signature
pain discovery may only use the venue's own evidence — manufactured dread is forbidden
positioning compares service models and never smears a named local competitor
disclosure-first selling forbids silent auto-renewal and exit fees detached from real cost
guest-data monetization is not a pricing lever; the fee must carry the service on its own
the verifiable-claim rule defines what may enter the proof kit at all
no proposal may ship without the survey contingency and coarse-observable labeling
thin restaurant margins press the quoted fee down toward and below the derived cost floor
edges.resolution_rule: the cost floor wins: reshape the deal to a lighter tier or decline it; the fee is never set below the derived floor to win a venue

edges.why_related: hardware recovery pressure pushes toward long punitive lock-ins that honest-exit terms forbid
edges.resolution_rule: recovery is protected by stated exit arithmetic — remaining amortization payoff or equipment buyout — never by silent renewal or punitive fees detached from real cost

edges.why_related: the drive to win the comparison collides with the gate's duty to concede when one-time install genuinely fits
edges.resolution_rule: the qualification verdict wins: when a one-time install or in-house IT genuinely fits the venue, the provider says so and offers an install or nothing

edges.why_related: restaurant marketing appetite for captured guest emails collides with the disclosed-collection commitment
edges.resolution_rule: the privacy stance wins: only disclosed, venue-agreed, guest-visible collection ships; undisclosed capture is refused even at the cost of the deal

edges.why_related: honest, checkable proof assets make partners willing to attach their reputation as referrers
one satisfied property-management account causes portfolio referrals across its other buildings
win/loss reasons from issued proposals recalibrate the derivation's components and margins
clustered no-go reasons are the error signal that re-ranks the beachhead map
both are multi-tenant building sales where the landlord-versus-tenant question decides the contract party

conflict_axes.name: recurring_value_vs_sticker_shock
conflict_axes.description: The subscription's lifecycle value collides with buyers anchored on a one-time install price; the monthly figure looks expensive next to a flyer even when the lifecycle math favors it.
poles: sell the full-service subscription at its derived price
shrink the monthly figure to defuse comparison
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: anchor on the venue's own outage cost and lifecycle total; move tiers, never move below the derived floor

conflict_axes.name: guest_story_vs_ops_story
conflict_axes.description: The visible guest-experience narrative opens conversations but commoditizes against consumer gear, while the operations-continuity narrative justifies the fee but is invisible until a failure.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: open with whichever story the venue class feels, but anchor the subscription on operations continuity before pricing is discussed

conflict_axes.name: deal_hunger_vs_honest_qualification
conflict_axes.description: A young provider's need for signed accounts presses against the gate's duty to decline misfit venues and concede deals where the offer adds no value.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: the gate record decides; a declined misfit costs one deal, a signed misfit costs margin, reputation and support capacity for a whole term

conflict_axes.name: portal_data_value_vs_guest_privacy
conflict_axes.description: Venues want marketing value from captured guest data while the productized privacy stance forbids undisclosed collection and any sale of guest data.
poles: minimize and disclose guest data collection
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: collection happens only with venue agreement and on-portal guest disclosure; refusal of undisclosed capture is absolute

conflict_axes.name: pre_survey_certainty_vs_site_truth
conflict_axes.description: Buyers demand a firm AP count and fixed price today while the building's spectrum, walls and cabling are facts only the survey will establish.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: give a labeled estimate range from coarse observables and let the disclosed survey contingency absorb what the building reveals

conflict_axes.name: hardware_recovery_vs_exit_fairness
conflict_axes.description: Fronted hardware must be recovered across the term, which tempts punitive lock-ins that the honest-exit position forbids.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: recover through stated amortization payoff or equipment buyout at exit; retention comes from service quality, not traps

conflict_axes.name: scope_generosity_vs_helpdesk_creep
conflict_axes.description: Being helpful on out-of-scope requests builds goodwill but erodes the boundary until the subscription funds an unpaid general IT helpdesk.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: one-time small favors are named as favors; recurring requests get quoted through the scope's change path, and the exclusion list grows to name new request classes

conflict_axes.name: beachhead_focus_vs_opportunism
conflict_axes.description: Discipline says concentrate on the ranked beachhead segments while attractive out-of-segment deals keep arriving through partners and walk-ins.
poles: take good deals wherever they appear
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: out-of-segment deals still pass the same gate; a pattern of good out-of-segment wins is a signal to re-rank the map, not to abandon it

conflict_axes.name: premium_promise_vs_staffable_reality
conflict_axes.description: Premium response commitments sell property-scale deals but must be honored by a small bench whose after-hours coverage is finite.
poles: promise the response the buyer wants
promise only what the bench can staff
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: the tier ladder offers only commitments the current bench demonstrably staffs; growth in the bench precedes growth in the promise

edge_cases.description: A tenant restaurant wants to sign but the lease gives the landlord control of building wiring and internet service
edge_cases.trigger: the signer lacks authority over the infrastructure the offer touches
edge_cases.mitigation: verify authority during qualification; obtain landlord consent in writing before proposal, or restructure the deal with the landlord as party

edge_cases.description: A buyer demands a firm AP count and fixed monthly price before any site visit has happened
edge_cases.trigger: pre-survey certainty is demanded as a condition of continuing
edge_cases.mitigation: give an estimate range labeled as walk-based with the survey contingency explained as protection for both sides; decline to fake certainty

edge_cases.description: A restaurant asks for the captive portal to harvest guest emails without telling the guests
edge_cases.trigger: a venue requests undisclosed guest data collection
edge_cases.mitigation: offer disclosed opt-in collection with on-portal notice; refuse undisclosed capture even if the deal walks

edge_cases.description: A motel prospect turns out to be inside an exclusive ISP-bundled Wi-Fi contract with years to run
edge_cases.trigger: an existing exclusive agreement blocks the deal regardless of merit
edge_cases.mitigation: check existing contracts during qualification; record the expiry and time a follow-up rather than inducing a breach

edge_cases.description: A venue equates managed Wi-Fi with internet service and expects the provider to answer for ISP outages
edge_cases.trigger: the demarcation was never explained before signature
edge_cases.mitigation: explain the demarcation and what an ISP outage will look like before signature, and define escalation help as a courtesy or add-on

edge_cases.description: A prospect asks 'what is your uptime?' and the young provider has no measured history to cite
edge_cases.trigger: a track-record question the provider cannot answer with data
edge_cases.mitigation: state plainly that measured history is short, show the monitoring method and the pilot's measured data, and offer the pilot owner as a reference; never invent a percentage

edge_cases.description: A thin-margin cafe's honest cost floor lands above what the venue can credibly pay
edge_cases.trigger: the derived floor exceeds the venue's economic reach
edge_cases.mitigation: offer the entry tier or a customer-owned-hardware structure; if no honest configuration clears the floor, decline rather than price below it

edge_cases.description: A franchise venue's corporate office mandates a national Wi-Fi standard and vendor list
edge_cases.trigger: a franchise mandate overrides the local owner's buying authority
edge_cases.mitigation: surface franchise mandates during qualification; pursue only if the offer can comply with the mandate or the mandate leaves local scope

edge_cases.description: Days from signature, the buyer asks to fold camera installation and a printer fix into the same monthly fee
edge_cases.mitigation: hold the scope sheet; quote adjacent work separately and note that expansion services on live accounts belong to a later conversation

edge_cases.description: An MDU board asks the provider to bill residents per unit, effectively making it a building internet reseller
edge_cases.trigger: the amenity framing is pushed toward a per-resident billed service
edge_cases.mitigation: recognize that reselling connectivity per resident may change the provider's regulatory class — an obligation class to verify in the operating jurisdiction — and keep the offer amenity-to-the-property unless prepared for that change

edge_cases.description: A promising partner demands an undisclosed kickback baked invisibly into the venue's monthly price
edge_cases.trigger: a referral partner requires concealment as a condition of the channel
edge_cases.mitigation: referral arrangements are disclosed to the venue or they do not exist; walk away from partners requiring concealment

edge_cases.description: A one-time installer's hardware-only flyer price makes the buyer ask why the managed offer costs monthly forever
edge_cases.trigger: a head-to-head comparison against a one-time price
edge_cases.mitigation: compare the lifecycle contents side by side — monitoring, fixes, replacement — without disparaging the installer, and concede honestly if a one-time install fits this venue

workflow.description: Fix the recurring accountabilities, the one-time components, and the managed site as the unit of sale
workflow.gate: recurring wrapper and one-time components are separated and the monthly accountabilities are listed in owner-repeatable language

workflow.description: Write the verifiable-claim, disclosure-first, no-fear-selling and small-buyer-care rules every pitch must obey
workflow.gate: each rule is stated with its forbidden counter-example and every current pitch claim traces to evidence

workflow.description: Commit in contract language to no interception, no sale of guest data, and disclosed captive-portal collection only
workflow.gate: no-interception and no-sale clauses exist, disclosed-collection is required, and the jurisdiction-check flag is present

workflow.action: Map and rank the target venue segments
workflow.description: Walk the local market and rank restaurant, lodging, office, retail and MDU classes by fit, radius and reachable buyers
workflow.artifact: venue segment map with beachhead ranking
workflow.gate: each class names its buyer, must-not-fail workload, scale band and beachhead position

workflow.action: Split the guest and operations value stories
workflow.description: Write both narratives with venue-recognizable failure examples and assign the subscription anchor to operations continuity
workflow.gate: both stories carry class-recognizable failure examples and the operations story carries the fee justification

workflow.action: Draw the management scope and demarcation
workflow.description: Write the inclusion and exclusion lists including the ISP boundary and the likely month-two requests
workflow.gate: inclusions, exclusions, ISP outages, endpoint devices and new cabling are all explicitly addressed

workflow.action: Build the price derivation and tier ladder
workflow.description: Define the per-site base and per-AP increment components, the per-deal cost-floor check, and the tier depths they price
workflow.artifact: price derivation worksheet and tier ladder
workflow.gate: cost-floor components are enumerated, tier contents are written, and no material asserts a specific monthly figure as fact

workflow.action: Choose funding models and term mechanics
workflow.description: Define the customer-owned, amortized and provider-owned options with their exit arithmetic and term implications
workflow.gate: each model states its exit outcome and the renewal clauses carry the jurisdiction-check flag

workflow.action: Run pain discovery on the live prospect
workflow.description: Collect the venue's dead zones, rush drops, review mentions and outage memory into a written evidence-based inventory
workflow.gate: every inventory item traces to a staff statement, review mention or dated incident

workflow.action: Qualify the deal at the gate
workflow.description: Check pain, floor clearance, radius, expectation fit, signing authority and blocking contracts, and record the verdict
workflow.gate: all six checks are answered with evidence and a no-go records its reason

workflow.description: Compose the pain summary, tier, transparent derivation, survey contingency, funding and term, scope, demarcation and privacy sections
workflow.gate: all required sections are present and signature triggers the survey handoff to the design KB with the proposal attached

priority_rationale: The frame and governance nodes — offer definition, segment map, value split, sales ethics, privacy stance — come first because every price, tier, contract clause and pitch downstream inherits their commitments; the offer-architecture chain (scope, price mechanism, tiers, funding, term, demarcation) must exist before any venue-shaped variant or live-deal artifact can be honest; and qualification, positioning and proposal assembly come last because they consume all of it to decide, per venue, whether to propose, what to propose, and when to walk away.

dominance_rules.rule: Disclosure-first ethics dominates every closing tactic
dominance_rules.rationale: one undisclosed term or invented claim can unwind a deal, poison local reputation and invite a dispute worth more than the account
dominance_rules.trigger: any pressure to close while a claim, term or fee mechanic remains undisclosed or unverifiable
dominance_rules.action: disclose or remove the claim before signature; no signature happens ahead of full disclosure

dominance_rules.rule: The guest-privacy commitment dominates venue marketing appetite
dominance_rules.rationale: undisclosed guest data collection breaches the productized stance and may breach data-protection obligations
dominance_rules.trigger: a venue or vendor requests interception, sale, or undisclosed captive-portal collection
dominance_rules.action: refuse; offer only disclosed, venue-agreed, guest-visible collection, and decline the deal if refusal ends it

dominance_rules.rule: The derived cost floor dominates competitive price pressure
dominance_rules.rationale: a below-floor account loses money every month of its term and cannot be fixed by volume
dominance_rules.trigger: a buyer or competitor comparison pushes the quote below the deal's derived floor
dominance_rules.action: reshape to a lighter tier or different funding model, or decline; never quote below the floor

dominance_rules.rule: The survey contingency dominates the demand for pre-survey certainty
dominance_rules.rationale: spectrum, walls and cabling are site facts the walk cannot establish, and faked certainty converts into margin loss or a trust-breaking walk-back
dominance_rules.trigger: a buyer demands a firm AP count or fixed price before the survey
dominance_rules.action: present the labeled estimate range with the contingency explained; do not issue uncontingent numbers

dominance_rules.rule: The written scope dominates verbal generosity
dominance_rules.rationale: unwritten promises accumulate into an unpaid IT helpdesk that the subscription never priced
dominance_rules.trigger: a request arrives for service outside the written inclusions
dominance_rules.action: answer from the scope sheet: a named one-time favor, a quoted change, or a referral — never a silent absorption

dominance_rules.rule: An honest no-go dominates pipeline hunger
dominance_rules.rationale: a signed misfit consumes install and support capacity for a full term and generates the town's worst references
dominance_rules.trigger: a deal fails any gate check but momentum says sign it anyway
dominance_rules.action: record the no-go with its reason and decline or restructure; the gate record is the decision

dominance_rules.rationale: a response promise the bench cannot honor at 2 a.m. converts a premium fee into a breached contract
dominance_rules.trigger: a deal wants a response commitment beyond the bench's demonstrated coverage
dominance_rules.action: offer the strongest staffable tier and decline the rest until the bench grows first

dominance_rules.rule: Mechanism honesty dominates the demand for a number
dominance_rules.rationale: invented uptime percentages and asserted market prices are fabrications that the first measured quarter exposes
dominance_rules.trigger: a buyer, partner or document requests a specific figure the provider has not derived or measured
dominance_rules.action: give the derivation or the measured value with its window, or state that the number does not exist yet

anti_rework_rules.rule: Write the offer definition and scope sheet before deriving any price
anti_rework_rules.prevents: re-quoting every open deal when the priced service turns out to be undefined or different per salesperson

anti_rework_rules.rule: Set the ethics and privacy rules before the first pitch is delivered
anti_rework_rules.prevents: retracting claims, rewriting portals and rebuilding trust after a commitment the rules would have forbidden

anti_rework_rules.rule: Verify signing authority — landlord versus tenant, owner versus franchise — before proposal effort
anti_rework_rules.prevents: complete proposals dying against a lease clause or franchise mandate no one checked

anti_rework_rules.rule: Collect the venue's own pain evidence before writing any value narrative for it
anti_rework_rules.prevents: generic pitches that must be rebuilt after the venue fails to recognize itself in them

anti_rework_rules.rule: Attach the survey contingency to the very first estimate a buyer sees
anti_rework_rules.prevents: renegotiating price and trust after the survey raises the AP count beyond the walked guess

anti_rework_rules.rule: Choose the hardware funding model before drafting term, renewal and exit clauses
anti_rework_rules.prevents: contract rewrites when the exit arithmetic contradicts who actually owns the ceiling APs

anti_rework_rules.rule: Explain the ISP demarcation before signature, not during the first outage
anti_rework_rules.prevents: emergency trust repair and scope disputes when the internet circuit fails on a live account

anti_rework_rules.rule: Check for blocking contracts — ISP bundles, franchise programs, exclusive building agreements — during qualification
anti_rework_rules.prevents: proposals and surveys spent on venues that were never legally able to sign

iteration_protocol.trigger: a proposal is lost with price named as the reason
iteration_protocol.action: re-examine the derivation's components and the tier fit for that venue class; adjust components or tiers, never breach the floor

iteration_protocol.trigger: post-survey findings repeatedly diverge from pre-sale walk estimates
iteration_protocol.action: recalibrate the coarse-observable heuristics and widen the labeled estimate range the walk produces

iteration_protocol.trigger: no-go verdicts or early problem accounts cluster in one venue class
iteration_protocol.action: re-rank the beachhead map and revise that class's shaping node with the observed failure pattern

iteration_protocol.trigger: live accounts generate out-of-scope requests the sheet does not address
iteration_protocol.action: extend the exclusion list to name the new request class and align the offer definition's language

iteration_protocol.trigger: privacy, consumer-disclosure or auto-renewal rules change in the operating jurisdiction
iteration_protocol.action: re-verify the privacy clauses and renewal mechanics against current rules and reissue affected templates

iteration_protocol.trigger: a partner channel produces leads that consistently fail qualification
iteration_protocol.action: rewrite the partner brief with the gate's criteria and adjust or end the arrangement

iteration_protocol.trigger: the first deployments produce measured before/after data
iteration_protocol.action: replace every assumed proof point in the kit with the measured dataset and permissioned references

iteration_protocol.trigger: a local competitor begins bundling monitoring or a managed rival enters the territory
iteration_protocol.action: refresh the positioning frame and re-check which segments the differentiation still holds in
